labs.tagline: Which sockets exist, and what state are they in?
labs.problem: Determine whether a service is listening, on which address, and what state every connection is in.
labs.how: Reads socket information directly from netlink. Replaces netstat and is much faster on hosts with many sockets.

flags.why: Listening sockets only — the 'is it up?' view.
TCP or UDP only.
Numeric ports and addresses; avoids lookups.
Show the owning process (needs privileges for other users' sockets).
TCP internal info: rtt, retransmits, cwnd — invaluable for latency.

examples.note: What is listening, on which address, with process names.
Retransmissions and RTT for one peer.
State census on a busy server.

labs.sample:
$ ss -ltnp
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN 0      128    0.0.0.0:22            0.0.0.0:*         users:(("sshd",pid=812,fd=3))
LISTEN 0      511    127.0.0.1:5432        0.0.0.0:*         users:(("postgres",pid=1204,fd=7))
LISTEN 0      511    [::]:443               [::]:*            users:(("nginx",pid=1330,fd=8))
read: Local Address shows the bind address: 0.0.0.0 (all IPv4), [::] (all IPv6), or a specific address.
A socket bound to 127.0.0.1 is unreachable from other hosts no matter what the firewall allows.
Recv-Q growing on a LISTEN socket can indicate an application not accepting connections fast enough.
States: LISTEN, ESTAB, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECV, TIME-WAIT, CLOSE-WAIT. Persistently many CLOSE-WAIT means an application leaking sockets; many TIME-WAIT is normal for the closing side.
mistakes: Forgetting -p, then not knowing which process owns the port.
Reading ESTAB as proof the application is healthy — it only proves a TCP connection exists.
Ignoring the bind address column and concluding 'it is listening' means 'it is reachable'.
labs.when: Whenever 'the port is closed', 'connections are hanging', or a server is running out of sockets.

try.scenario: Inventory listening TCP sockets and their owning processes, and count socket states.
try.task: List listeners with process names, then summarise connection states.
try.command: ss -ltnp; echo ---; ss -tan | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
try.verdict_ok: You have listeners plus a state census — the standard baseline for a socket investigation.
try.verdict_missing: Paste the LISTEN table and the state counts; the census needs the awk/sort pipeline output.

simulate.intro: A remote user cannot reach PostgreSQL on port 5432. Read the output.
simulate.terminal:
$ ss -ltnp
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN 0      128    0.0.0.0:22            0.0.0.0:*         users:(("sshd",pid=812,fd=3))
LISTEN 0      511    127.0.0.1:5432        0.0.0.0:*         users:(("postgres",pid=1204,fd=7))
LISTEN 0      511    [::]:443               [::]:*            users:(("nginx",pid=1330,fd=8))

questions.prompt: Why can a remote client not connect to 5432?
options: Port 5432 is closed by the firewall
PostgreSQL is bound to 127.0.0.1 only, so it never accepts traffic from the network
questions.explanation: The bind address is the loopback, so packets arriving on the external interface have no listener — the kernel sends RST.

why_wrong.2: A firewall DROP would give a timeout; and the binding already explains refusal.
why_wrong.0: The bind address excludes all external families here.

questions.prompt: What would the client see if a firewall dropped the traffic instead?
options: A hang ending in 'connection timed out'
questions.explanation: DROP produces silence, so the client waits and times out. RST produces immediate refusal.

why_wrong.1: No name resolution occurs at that stage.

apply.scenario: A web server has thousands of connections in CLOSE-WAIT and memory keeps rising.
apply.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: The application is not closing sockets, so descriptors accumulate and exhaust limits
apply.explanation: CLOSE-WAIT means the peer closed and the local application has not called close(). The bug is in the application.

why_wrong.3: SYN floods create SYN-RECV, not CLOSE-WAIT.
why_wrong.0: The state has a specific meaning at the application layer.
why_wrong.1: Retransmissions show in ss -ti, not as CLOSE-WAIT.

labs.tagline: The legacy tool — know it, prefer ss.
labs.problem: You are on a machine where net-tools is installed and ss is not, and you still need socket and route data.
labs.how: Reads /proc/net. Slower than ss and deprecated on Fedora (net-tools is not installed by default).

flags.why: TCP or UDP.
Listening.
Numeric.
Process. Note: -p on netstat also sets promiscuous mode semantics historically; here it shows PIDs.
Routing table (use ip route instead).

labs.sample:
$ netstat -tlnp
Proto Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address      Foreign Address    State    PID/Program name
tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:22         0.0.0.0:*          LISTEN   812/sshd
tcp        0      0 127.0.0.1:5432     0.0.0.0:*          LISTEN   1204/postgres
read: Same information as ss, different layout: Proto, Recv-Q, Send-Q, Local Address, Foreign Address, State, PID/Program.
The PID/Program column needs root for other users' sockets, exactly like ss -p.
The mapping to modern tools: netstat -tlnp = ss -ltnp, netstat -rn = ip route, netstat -i = ip -s link.
mistakes: Assuming netstat is installed on Fedora — it is a separate package (net-tools) that is no longer default.
Using netstat on hosts with huge socket tables; it is significantly slower than ss.
Writing new scripts against netstat output.
labs.when: Only when ss is unavailable. Otherwise use ss.

try.scenario: Check whether net-tools exists on your system, and capture the ss equivalent of the same query.
try.task: Test for netstat, then run the modern equivalent either way.
try.command: command -v netstat && netstat -tlnp | head -5 || echo 'net-tools not installed'; echo ---; ss -ltnp | head -5

expected_patterns.label: either a clear absence message or listener output

try.verdict_ok: You established tool availability and produced the modern equivalent.
try.verdict_missing: Paste both parts; the point is the presence/absence of netstat plus the ss output.

simulate.intro: Translate this legacy output into the modern equivalents.
simulate.terminal:
$ netstat -rn
Kernel IP routing table
Destination   Gateway         Genmask         Flags Metric Iface
0.0.0.0       10.0.0.1        0.0.0.0         UG    100    eth0
10.0.0.0      0.0.0.0         255.255.255.0   U     100    eth0

questions.prompt: Which modern command shows the same routing information?
questions.explanation: ip route prints the same table with clearer semantics (cisco-style flags are gone).

why_wrong.3: ss has no routing table view.

questions.prompt: What does the UG flag mean on the first line?
options: Route is Up and uses a Gateway — i.e. the default route
questions.explanation: U = up, G = gateway. The destination 0.0.0.0 with a gateway is the default route.

apply.scenario: A runbook tells you to run `netstat -tlnp` on a fresh Fedora 45 server and it fails with 'command not found'.
apply.question: What is the correct response?
options: Run the runbook on another OS
Install net-tools and never mention ss
Use ss -ltnp — net-tools is not installed by default, and installing it is unnecessary
apply.explanation: ss is the supported replacement and is present by default. Updating the runbook is the durable fix.

why_wrong.2: Adds a dependency for no benefit.

labs.tagline: Ground truth for 'are packets actually flowing?'
labs.problem: Settle definitively whether traffic leaves, arrives, or is answered — and identify the TCP-level failure.
labs.how: Uses libpcap to copy frames from the interface into user space, filtered by a BPF expression. Requires root or CAP_NET_RAW.

flags.why: Interface, or 'any' where supported.
Stop after N packets. Always bound a capture.
No name/port resolution. Faster and avoids surprise DNS.
Show link-layer headers (MAC addresses).
Write a pcap instead of flooding the terminal.
Payload as ASCII / hex+ASCII. Be careful with sensitive data.

examples.cmd: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -c 20 'tcp port 443 and host 203.0.113.20'

read: S, S., . is a complete handshake. S repeated with no reply means packets leave and nothing returns.
S followed by R means refusal. S followed by ICMP unreachable means no route or an administrative block.
Repeated identical sequence numbers indicate retransmission, i.e. loss in one direction.
An R mid-session means something tore down an established connection: firewall state, idle timeout, or a crash.
mistakes: Capturing without a count or filter on a busy link — you can fill the disk or lose the terminal.
Pasting raw captures into tickets without redacting addresses and payloads.
Running captures on the wrong interface (the VPN's tun0 rather than eth0), then concluding nothing is happening.
labs.when: When logs and counters are inconclusive and you need packet-level evidence.

try.scenario: Capture a bounded DNS exchange while making one lookup, and identify whether responses come back.
try.task: Start a short capture filtered to port 53 in one terminal, make a lookup, and paste the capture.
try.command: sudo tcpdump -i any -n -c 6 'port 53' & sleep 1; dig example.com +short; wait

expected_patterns.label: TCP flags or a DNS query marker

try.verdict_ok: You captured a query and a response — the packet-level proof that resolution traffic is flowing both ways.
try.verdict_missing: Paste the capture lines. You may need sudo, or to choose the interface carrying your DNS traffic.

simulate.intro: Port 443 appears unreachable. This is the capture.

options: The server's application is refusing connections
SYNs leave the client with no reply: the cause is downstream (filter, route or dead host)
questions.explanation: Identical SYNs retransmitted with no SYN-ACK or RST: the request goes out and nothing comes back.

questions.prompt: Which is the most useful next investigation?
options: Reinstall the application on the server
Check the path and filters: traceroute -T -p 443 and the destination's firewall/security group
questions.explanation: The evidence points to drop on the path or at the destination, so establish where the packets stop.

why_wrong.0: The server's stack may not even see the SYNs.

apply.scenario: A capture shows a completed handshake, then the client sends data and receives R after 300 seconds.
apply.question: What is the most plausible interpretation?
options: A stateful device or the application closed an idle connection — check firewall idle timeouts and keepalive settings
apply.explanation: A reset after a long-lived connection is typically an idle timeout in a firewall/NAT or an application policy.

why_wrong.1: The handshake completed, so a listener exists.
why_wrong.0: Traffic flowed both ways for a while.

labs.tagline: Test the whole stack: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP.
labs.problem: Determine whether a service is reachable and functional, and read the exact error when it is not.
labs.how: Performs name resolution, connects, performs TLS when applicable, and exchanges an HTTP request. Verbose mode shows each stage separately.

flags.why: Show DNS, connect, TLS and request stages — the single most useful diagnostic flag.
HEAD request: headers only, does not transfer the body.
Bound the connect phase so a black hole does not hang you.
Skip certificate verification (diagnosis only, never in production code).
Override DNS to test one address while keeping the Host header.
Status code only, useful in scripts.

examples.note: Bypass DNS, keep the SNI/Host header.

labs.sample:
$ curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://wiki.corp.example/
* Host wiki.corp.example:443 was resolved.
*   Trying 10.10.5.20:443...
* Connected to wiki.corp.example (10.10.5.20) port 443
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1)
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / AEAD-AES256-GCM-SHA384
* Server certificate: CN=wiki.corp.example
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
read: 'was resolved' proves DNS worked. If that line is missing or says 'Could not resolve host', the failure is naming.
'Trying ...' with no 'Connected' means the TCP handshake never completed: timeout or drop.
'Connection refused' means RST: nothing listening on that port/address.
TLS errors after 'Connected' are certificate or protocol problems, not network reachability.
The HTTP status is the application layer; a 502 means the reverse proxy could not reach a backend.
mistakes: Using curl -k to 'fix' a certificate problem rather than reading the error.
Not bounding connect time, so a black-holed path hangs for minutes.
Concluding 'the service is down' from a 403 — that is authorisation, not availability.
labs.when: As soon as you know the name resolves, to test transport and application in one step.

try.scenario: Test a public HTTPS endpoint in a bounded way and capture the staged evidence.
try.task: Run a verbose, time-bounded request and identify the resolved IP, the TLS version and the status code.
try.verdict_ok: You have resolution, transport/TLS and the HTTP status — a complete staged result.
try.verdict_missing: Paste the verbose output including the HTTP status line (use -v and keep stderr).

simulate.intro: Three requests to the same service fail differently. Diagnose each.
simulate.terminal:
$ curl -sv --connect-timeout 3 https://app.corp.example/ 2>&1 | head -4
* Could not resolve host: app.corp.example

$ curl -sv --connect-timeout 3 https://10.10.5.30:443/ 2>&1 | head -5
*   Trying 10.10.5.30:443...
* connect to 10.10.5.30 port 443 failed: Connection refused

$ curl -sv --connect-timeout 3 https://10.10.5.40:443/ 2>&1 | head -4
*   Trying 10.10.5.40:443...
* Connection timed out after 3001 milliseconds

questions.prompt: Which failure is a naming problem?
questions.explanation: No resolution occurred, so no packet was sent. Check NSS, hosts, resolver config and the record.

why_wrong.2: That reached the host and got RST.
why_wrong.1: That reached the network but got silence.

questions.prompt: For the third host, what is proven?
options: SYNs left the client and nothing came back — filter, wrong route, or a dead host
questions.explanation: A timeout means silence: no RST, no SYN-ACK. That is a drop or an unreachable host.

apply.scenario: curl to https://app:443 connects, TLS completes, and the response is HTTP 502.
apply.question: Where is the fault?
options: The front-end is reachable but cannot reach its backend — an application/proxy problem, not a network path problem
The client cannot resolve the name
apply.explanation: DNS, TCP and TLS all succeeded. A 502 comes from the proxy reporting a backend failure.

labs.problem: Test whether a specific TCP or UDP port is reachable, without HTTP or TLS in the way.
labs.how: Opens a TCP connection (or sends UDP datagrams) and reports success or the precise error. With -l it can listen, which is useful for lab tests.

flags.why: Scan mode: connect and close without sending data.
Verbose: report open/refused explicitly.
Timeout in seconds — essential for timeouts vs refusals.
UDP instead of TCP (note: absence of a reply is not proof of a closed port).
Listen mode, for testing from the other side.

examples.note: Listen locally to prove egress from another host.

labs.sample:
$ nc -vz -w 3 10.0.0.5 22
Connection to 10.0.0.5 22 port [tcp/ssh] succeeded!

$ nc -vz -w 3 10.0.0.5 8080
nc: connect to 10.0.0.5 port 8080 (tcp) failed: Connection refused

$ nc -vz -w 3 10.0.0.9 443
nc: connect to 10.0.0.9 port 443 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress
read: 'succeeded' means the TCP handshake completed: a listener exists and the path works.
'Connection refused' means RST: the host is reachable but nothing listens on that port/address.
'timed out' means silence: a DROP rule, wrong route, or dead host.
For UDP, no output usually means 'sent, no reply' — which does not prove the port is closed.
mistakes: Using nc -u to conclude a UDP port is closed (you usually cannot know).
Omitting -w, so a filtered port hangs the terminal.
Testing from a host that is allowed by policy and assuming the user's position is identical.
labs.when: When you need the port-level answer without protocol complexity.

try.scenario: Test a real port on a public host to see the difference between open and refused.
try.task: Test TCP 443 and a port that is very likely closed, with a short timeout.

expected_patterns.label: a failure line for the closed port

try.verdict_ok: You have both signatures side by side: success on an open port and a precise failure on a closed one.
try.verdict_missing: Paste both probe results including the error text; that contrast is the lesson.

simulate.intro: Two probes to the same server. Interpret both.
simulate.terminal:
$ nc -vz -w 3 203.0.113.20 443
Connection to 203.0.113.20 443 port [tcp/https] succeeded!
$ nc -vz -w 3 203.0.113.20 8080
nc: connect to 203.0.113.20 port 8080 (tcp) timed out

questions.prompt: What is the difference in meaning between the two results?
options: 443 has a listening service; 8080 receives no response at all, suggesting a filter rather than an absent listener
questions.explanation: A closed port on a reachable host answers with RST (refused). Silence means packets were dropped — a filter.

questions.prompt: Which check would confirm a listener exists on 443 from the server side?
questions.explanation: ss shows the listener and the process owning it.

why_wrong.2: Only proves the client's path choice.

apply.scenario: A user cannot reach an application on port 8443. From your machine nc succeeds; from theirs it times out.
apply.question: What does this establish?
options: The service is up; the difference is path or policy specific to the user's location
apply.explanation: A successful connection from one place proves the listener exists; a timeout elsewhere is a filtering or routing difference on that path.
